title: Neuter insects of one nest should show graded structural differences

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Neuter insects of one nest should show graded structural differences

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: If worker modifications spread gradually through selection of fertile parents, sterile workers of the same species in the same nest should sometimes show gradations of structure, and such gradations are in fact often found.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: On this view we ought occasionally to find neuter-insects of the same species, in the same nest, presenting gradations of structure; and this we do find, even often

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VII, “Instinct”; section “Neuter or sterile insects”. Scope: worker castes of ants and other social insects

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch07-13: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The stated morphological prediction is direct and testable with specimen images and measurements. The observation alone does not prove the proposed selection mechanism, but it resolves the prediction.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure worker morphology within nests and test whether trait distributions contain continuous or graded intermediates between worker forms. Frequent within-nest intermediates support the prediction; consistently discrete distributions across adequately sampled species oppose it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Developmental plasticity can produce grades without documenting their evolutionary origin.

Specimen records may not always preserve nest identity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.78
data existence: 0.76
data adequacy: 0.58
operationalizability: 0.94
discriminating power: 0.82

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Within-nest morphometrics are a direct test of the prediction that neuters in one nest sometimes grade into each other, and ant specimen data make a start. Colony context is incomplete, so adequacy and feasibility stay moderate, and the link from gradation to selection on parents is an extra inference. The frequency word 'often' needs a broader sample than the famous polymorphic genera.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within single nests, test whether worker size and shape are continuously graded or fall into discrete modes, and estimate how often graded nests occur across species. Frequent within-nest gradations confirm the empirical clause; exclusively discrete castes with no graded species would refute the 'often' claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Bees, wasps, and termites are far less measured than ants.

Many AntWeb specimens lack a same-nest identifier, so within-nest series must be filtered by hand.

Continuous variation can be nutrition rather than the selective gradation the theory invokes.

data existence: 0.55
